# Acromioclavicular joint injury

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Upper extremity > Acromioclavicular joint injury*

[Original Article Link](/library/Q30uRf)

---

## Summary

<u>Acromioclavicular joint</u> injury is usually caused by direct injury to the <u>acromion</u> during a fall on an <u>adducted</u> arm. It is classified according to the <u>Rockwood classification</u>, which considers the extent of injury to the acromioclavicular (AC) <u>ligament</u> and the coracoclavicular (CC) <u>ligament</u>, as well as the displacement of the <u>clavicle</u> and type of <u>dislocation</u> in the <u>AC joint</u>. Patients present with local tenderness, swelling, limited <u>range of motion</u>, and/or deformity of the <u>joint</u>. <u>X-ray</u> is used to diagnose <u>joint</u> subluxation and clavicular displacement. Treatment is usually conservative and may include rest and <u>analgesia</u> for a few weeks. <u>Surgery</u> is recommended for more severe injuries when <u>ligament</u> repair is required.

---

## Etiology

* Most common: direct force injury to the superior aspect of the <u>acromion</u> while the arm is <u>adducted</u> (e.g., a fall while cycling or riding a horse)

* Less common: indirect injury via falling on an outstretched hand, which transmits force up the arm through the <u>humerus</u> to the <u>acromion</u>, causing displacement that distresses the AC <u>ligaments</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Local tenderness, swelling, and/or <u>bruising</u>

* <u>Pain</u> is elicited by the cross-body adduction test, in which the patient elevates their arm to 90° and actively <u>adducts</u> it across their body.

* Limited <u>range of motion of the shoulder</u> <u>joint</u>

* Visible deformity of the <u>lateral</u> aspect of the <u>clavicle</u> may be seen in types III and above

## Diagnosis

* Approach: <u>AC joint</u> injury is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> that can be classified according to the <u>Rockwood classification</u> via <u>x-ray</u>. If <u>x-ray</u> findings are questionable, an <u>MRI</u>, CT, or possibly <u>ultrasound</u> may be considered.

* Classification





| <br>Rockwood classification of AC joint injury<br> |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Injury type | AC <u>ligament</u> | <u>Joint capsule</u> | CC <u>ligament</u> | <u>Distal</u> <u>clavicle</u> | Deltoid and <u>trapezius</u> muscles |
| Type I | <br>* Sprained<br><br> | <br>* Intact<br><br> | <br>* Intact<br><br> | <br>* Intact<br><br> | <br>* Intact<br><br> |
| Type II | <br>* Ruptured<br><br> |  | <br>* Sprained<br><br> | <br>* <u>AC joint</u> widening and minimal elevation<br><br> | <br>* Possibly partial detachment from <u>clavicle</u><br><br> |
| Type III | <br>* Ruptured<br><br> |  |  | <br><br>* Moderately elevated and unstable to <u>stress</u><br><br>* Reducible (“piano key” sign)<br><br><br> | <br>* Likely detached from <u>distal</u> <u>clavicle</u><br><br> |
| Type IV | <br>* Ruptured<br><br> |  |  | <br><br>* Posteriorly displaced through the <u>trapezius</u><br><br>* Not reducible<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Likely detached from <u>distal</u> <u>clavicle</u><br><br>* Deltotrapezial <u>fascia</u> displaced<br><br><br> |
| Type V | <br>* Ruptured<br><br> |  |  | <br><br>* Severely elevated<br><br>* Not reducible<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Detached from <u>distal</u> <u>clavicle</u><br><br>* Deltotrapezial <u>fascia</u> ruptured<br><br><br> |
| Type VI (rare) | <br>* Ruptured<br><br> |  |  | <br>* Inferiorly displaced in subcoracoid position<br><br> | <br>* Usually detached from <u>clavicle</u><br><br> |





![Rockwood classification of acromioclavicular injury (types I-VI)](media/vjm4fj7e03f1zjq6rlnzgqnj.jpg)

Rockwood classification of acromioclavicular injury (types I-VI)

![Piano key sign (spring test)](media/nwtgo6hlyk3v0gtq3zc6q9zv.jpg)

Piano key sign (spring test)



* <u>X-ray</u> (<u>anterior</u>-<u>posterior</u> view, oblique view, axillary view) of the <u>shoulder joint</u>, <u>acromion</u>, and <u>scapula</u>: 

* Subluxation of the <u>AC joint</u> space

* Widening of the CC space

* Displacement of the <u>clavicle</u>

* Accompanying injuries (e.g., <u>clavicle fracture</u>)

* Chronic cases: features of AC <u>arthritis</u>, <u>distal</u> <u>clavicle</u> <u>osteolysis</u>

## Treatment

### Acute management




#### <u>Conservative treatment</u>




* Indications: types I and II

* Methods

* Sling for comfort: 1–3 weeks (e.g., Desault or <u>Gilchrist bandage</u>)

* Avoid heavy lifting

* <u>Analgesia</u> (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>)





#### Surgical treatment




* Indications

* Types III and above

* Management of type III is controversial and determined on an individual basis

* All patients with type III and above should be referred to an orthopedist

* <u>Open fractures</u>

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u>

* Failed <u>conservative treatment</u>

* Objective: <u>ligament</u> repair and reconstruction

* Methods

* <u>Arthroscopic</u> (all or assisted): preferred as less invasive

* Open <u>surgery</u>





### Long-term management




* Indications

* Persistent <u>pain</u> after healing of initial <u>ligamentous injury</u>

* Repeated minor injury without instability but persistent <u>AC joint</u> <u>arthralgia</u>

* Methods

* Avoiding painful movement and <u>analgesia</u>

* Intraarticular <u>glucocorticoid</u> injections
